source.title: Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models with Synthetic Data
source.authors: Hirokazu Kiyomaru; Yusuke Oda; Takashi Kodama; Chao-Hong Liu; Daisuke Kawahara

record.file_problem: The full paper is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares Japanese downstream benchmark performance across three model sizes, a different measure from the held-out pretraining loss in the scaling-law claim. It does not fit or test a power law.
record.gate_note: The paper reports no held-out cross-entropy loss, power-law fits, or predictions from small runs. It does report aggregate downstream scores at three model sizes, which bear on V6. Hoffmann et al. is cited to contextualize the fixed token budget, not tested here. The paper also compares corpus mixtures, but those results do not test the other claim versions.
record.test_reason: Scaling is not the paper's question. It is a Japanese data-augmentation study at a fixed 72B-token budget, but it reports downstream averages at 1.8B, 3.8B and 7.2B parameters for six corpus mixtures, pre-trained and fine-tuned. That bears weakly on V6 in a new setting: non-English, data-constrained, 4x size range, no fit. T3 fits better than T2 because the study is not aimed at the scaling question. Token count is fixed, so the larger models are increasingly under-trained (about 2x, 1x and 0.5x Chinchilla-optimal), which confounds the size comparison. No loss, power-law fit, extrapolation, allocation or shape test exists for V1–V5 or V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that paraphrase and instruction-style synthetic Japanese corpora give the strongest downstream gains under data scarcity across model sizes, often matching or beating additional organic text. These gains persist after fine-tuning, suggesting better general language modelling. Partial synthesis plus moderate epochs approaches full-synthesis performance. They draw no conclusion about scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares fixed-token corpus mixtures and downstream benchmark scores across three model sizes; it does not use the original scaling-law loss measurement or fit power laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream average scores vary with corpus mixture and training stage; the model-size trend for JA-Web-9B is non-monotonic. The paper also reports a scale-dependent comparison between translation and direct English data.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed 72B-token budget, paraphrase and instruction-style synthetic Japanese corpora beat repeated Japanese Web and English Web text, and match or exceed additional organic Japanese text.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Synthetic rephrasing of scarce target-language data substitutes for unique organic tokens in data-constrained pre-training.

fits_no_version.finding: The advantage of translated English over raw English shrinks with model size: clear at 1.8B (.4112 vs .3472), much smaller at 3.8B and 7.2B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger models need less explicit translation for cross-lingual transfer.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Findings of EACL 2026)
record.problems: Only three model sizes are tested, and there are no held-out loss measurements, fitted predictions, uncertainty estimates, or reported statistical tests for the downstream comparisons. The paper notes that its synthetic corpora use only Qwen3-14B and that the study covers only Japanese. Fine-tuning uses aggregated benchmark training splits, including datasets evaluated in the study.
record.rows_left_out: Kept the AVG aggregate scores in Tables 1 and 2 for each corpus, model size, and training stage. Omitted the per-task JSQuAD, NIILC, JEMHopQA, and ALT values because the 60-row limit would be exceeded; the paper also provides partial-synthesis curves for 1.8B models in Figure 5, but no exact endpoint scores in the text or tables. These omissions do not provide held-out loss or power-law fits.

untested.parts: Relation of downstream scores to pretraining loss; whether the improvement follows a predictable functional form, or can be extrapolated; scale beyond a 4x parameter range; scale at a constant tokens-per-parameter ratio.
No held-out loss or power-law fit.
No compute-optimal allocation search; the Chinchilla ratios are only cited.
No power-law form tested for repeated data, fine-tuning or other modalities.
No fitted exponents or comparison of fitting choices.

missing.what: Per-task scores across sizes are often non-monotonic even where AVG rises. Examples: JA-Web-9B JSQuAD .43→.31→.22; EN-Web JSQuAD .42→.40 at 7.2B; JA-Instruct JEMHopQA .36→.30; JA-Paraphrase JEMHopQA .42→.34→.43. This bears on the per-task predictability part of V6.
Downstream average score curves against trained tokens for each size and corpus; shown as figures only, without numbers.

record.verdict_notes: Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited only as context. The size comparison is confounded by the fixed token budget: tokens per parameter fall from about 40 to about 10. The 1.8B–7.2B range spans under one order of magnitude, there are no uncertainty estimates, and fine-tuning uses the benchmarks' training splits. Treat the V6 labels as weak evidence.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law scaling in parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
No small-run fit is used to predict larger runs.
No compute budget is used to find loss-minimizing parameter and token allocations; token budget is fixed and downstream scores are measured.
No controlled comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study uses Japanese text, repeated data, and fine-tuning, but does not test whether a power-law form holds in these settings or in other modalities.
Reports downstream benchmark scores for three model sizes, but does not relate them to pretraining loss or fit a predictive relationship; tests only the reported Japanese task aggregate and settings.
No scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits are fitted or compared across fitting choices.

relationships.condition: The five 63B-augmentation corpora (EN-Web, JA-Paraphrase, JA-Instruct, JA-Translate, JA-Web), pre-trained and fine-tuned, 1.8B–7.2B at 72B tokens
relationships.reason: AVG rises monotonically with size in all ten condition groups (e.g. T3-P .50→.51→.58, T6-P .46→.50→.52). Several steps are small (T2-P-72, T4-P-72, T4-F-38, T6-F-72), and only three sizes are tested with no fit.
relationships.display_finding: Benchmark averages increased monotonically across all ten corpus-and-training settings, including sequences of 0.50→0.51→0.58 and 0.46→0.50→0.52, although several size steps yielded small gains.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: The five 63B-augmentation corpora (EN-Web, JA-Paraphrase, JA-Instruct, JA-Translate, JA-Web), pre-trained and fine-tuned, 1.8B–7.2B at 72B tokens
source_check.reason: Tables 1–2 show monotonically increasing AVG across all three sizes in all ten groups. This supports the direction of V6 within the tested range; quantitative prediction is untested.

relationships.condition: JA-Web-9B repeated for 8 epochs, at fixed 72B tokens
relationships.reason: Pre-trained AVG falls from 1.8B to 3.8B (.4099→.3396) and 7.2B stays below 1.8B (.3664). Fine-tuned AVG falls from 3.8B to 7.2B (.6519→.6392). Size gains fail under heavy data repetition (T1-P-38, T1-P-72, T1-F-72).
relationships.display_finding: Pretrained average scores fell from 0.4099 at 1.8B to 0.3396 at 3.8B and recovered only to 0.3664 at 7.2B, while fine-tuned averages fell 0.6519→0.6392 from 3.8B to 7.2B.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: JA-Web-9B repeated for 8 epochs, at fixed 72B tokens
source_check.reason: The grouped setting has mixed size effects: pre-trained AVG is .4099/.3396/.3664, while fine-tuned AVG is .6081/.6519/.6392. T1-P-38 and T1-P-72 undermine overall pre-training size gains; fine-tuning improves overall but reverses at the largest step. This qualifies V6 for the combined condition group.

relation.reason: Its own downstream measurements across model sizes bear on V6, although it fits no scaling law.

tranche.reason: The central question concerns corpus augmentation in Japanese under data scarcity. Tables 1–2 additionally report downstream results across three model sizes, bearing on V6 in this new setting.
